claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Pulumi supports authoring infrastructure in general-purpose languages (with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management), plus YAML and HCL.

Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready before dependent resources are created, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm applies resources in a fixed order determined by Kubernetes kind (per kind_sorter.go in the Helm source), not by declared dependencies.
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or between subcharts, except through hook weights.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK available in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only, and other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with policy rules written in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management on top of Pulumi Policies.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0, and Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's hardcoded install-order list of Kubernetes kinds begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so a chart cannot express installing a database subchart before an application subchart or starting a Deployment after a Job completes.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi's parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider's `helm.v4.Chart` resource supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only; a chart can install Custom Resource Definitions, workloads, and services, but resources outside the cluster need another tool.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and users roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release, while Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (orchestrating a production-ready cluster end-to-end, and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments that combine Pulumi and Helm.
A single Pulumi program can create an EKS, AKS, or GKE cluster, configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide (/docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/) walks through the end-to-end pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm charts.

Pulumi resolves chart `values` (including resource outputs such as an `aws.rds.Instance` connection string, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID) at deploy time and orders/installs the chart after the resources it depends on.
The FAQ section 'What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?' exists on the page at anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.

Pulumi's Automation API is an embeddable SDK for driving deployments from a host application, such as an internal developer platform, a SaaS product, or ephemeral preview environments per pull request.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, which can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for adopting Pulumi alongside Helm.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring already-provisioned in-cluster Kubernetes resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and a Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider's Helm chart resources accept values as typed Pulumi inputs, including outputs from other Pulumi resources.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Declaring a subchart as a Helm dependency does not make it install first, because Helm merges objects from a chart and all its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order; ordering within a release requires chart hooks with hook weights or application logic.
The page contains a section 'Resource ordering and dependencies' at anchor #resource-ordering-and-dependencies.
The page contains a section 'Adoption: coexistence, conversion, and import' at anchor #adoption-coexistence-conversion-and-import.
The Pulumi chart `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
